idiom_name: caller-owned capacity + realloc to the live length
implementation_notes: C has no container type that owns its capacity: the caller keeps the length and the capacity next to a heap block, so the pattern is that bookkeeping plus the reallocation - when the growth phase ends, call realloc(buf, len * sizeof *buf) and record the new capacity. realloc contracts the block in place when the allocator can and otherwise allocates a smaller block, copies the live prefix and frees the old one, so the trim is at worst O(len) and can fail, in which case the original block is still valid. Shrinking to zero elements is not a realloc at all - realloc(p, 0) is implementation-defined before C23 and undefined from C23, so free the block instead. Hand-rolled vectors (a struct with buf/len/cap and a vec_shrink_to_fit helper) are the shape this idiom takes; when the storage is arena- or pool-owned, the trim belongs to the arena and not to this code.
pitfalls: Assigning realloc's result straight back to the buffer leaks or loses the original block: on failure realloc returns NULL and leaves the old pointer valid, so assign to a temporary and only overwrite on success.
realloc(p, 0) is not 'shrink to nothing': it is implementation-defined before C23 and undefined behaviour from C23 - free the block explicitly for the empty case.

Contracting memory returns it to the allocator's arena, not necessarily to the operating system: RSS can stay flat after a successful trim, because trim thresholds and mmap breakpoints decide when pages go back.
sources: cppreference, realloc - 'The reallocation is done by either: a) expanding or contracting the existing area pointed to by ptr, if possible ... b) allocating a new memory block ... copying memory area with size equal the lesser of the new and the old sizes, and freeing the old block'; 'On failure, returns a null pointer. The original pointer ptr remains valid'; new_size zero is implementation-defined before C23 and undefined since C23: https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/memory/realloc
